A job board for service.

A free yoga class needs an extra pair of hands. A neighbor has time to spare. Public Horses gives them a way to help.

Our name comes from a teaching about a village that pooled its money for a horse anyone could use. That horse is our example of lifelong service.

Follow the yoga class request

Put the organization’s name on the request.

In My projects, the organizer creates an Organization profile. They add its public name, website, and a short description.

They choose that profile each time they want to post for the organization. Approved requests appear under the organization’s name.

Manage your listings.

The signed-in organizer sees the profiles and requests they manage in one workspace.

Draft
Edit the request and submit it for review.
Under review
Check its status. Read and act on the reviewer’s notes.
Published
Open the public listing. Mark it fulfilled when the team meets the need, or close it.

Twelve mats before class.

Yoga Studies Institute students started Lady Niguma Mexico to bring free yoga classes to a community near Mexico City.

In the demo, the organizer asks for help setting out 12 mats and greeting new students. A reviewer checks the request.

Yoga Studies Institute’s archived Yogi Corps profiles

A neighbor has 45 minutes.

They look for ways to give time near Mexico City. The listing tells them where to meet the teacher.

The board also shows chair yoga in Kansas and yoga for older adults in Romania. A project from Denmark brings yogic seed syllables into music lessons.

They offer to help.

They click Offer time. On a live listing, that opens the organizer’s own page so they can work out the details directly.

In the demo, the offer appears under My activity.

The room is ready.

In the demo, the organizer reports that the team set out 12 mats and helped new students settle in. The request moves to Completed.

What did I set in motion?

After the class, the neighbor records what they did and chooses an intention. They get a seed they can plant in their private garden.

They can come back and ask what changed after they helped.

“Two people stayed to talk to the teacher. Next time I’ll say hello before class.”

From the demo journal

Water the good you did.

We become gardeners of our own minds. Each act of service plants a karmic seed for the world we want to be part of.

To water it, first remember emptiness. The act arose through causes and conditions. Then remember what you gave and rejoice in the good you did.

Start with one community class.

We’d start with one organizer and one class. Your support would cover the time to post the first request and follow up with volunteers.

Did the class get the help it needed?
Ask the organizer what got done.
Did people come back?
With their permission, invite the same helpers to a second task. Ask the organizer how many completed it.
